meta.title: Anti-Money Laundering, Counter Financing of Terrorism, and Know Your Customer
meta.description: Comprehensive course on AML/CFT/KYC regulations, processes, and case studies based on the Access Bank ELTP Study Guide and AML Revised Participants Manual.

questionBank.q: A bank's client generated funds through counterfeit-goods sales and now routes the proceeds through legitimate-looking transactions. What is this activity called?
opts: Consolidating separate streams of legal income
Cleaning the proceeds of an illegal business
Restructuring an existing legitimate debt obligation
Reinvesting ordinary profits generated from lawful trading activity
questionBank.exp: Money laundering is defined as cleaning the proceeds of illegal business (dirty money) plus concealment of the underlying crime. The distractors describe ordinary, lawful financial activity of comparable specificity.

questionBank.q: What does Anti-Money Laundering (AML) refer to?
opts: A high-value corporate banking product line
Laws and procedures against disguising dirty money
A voluntary branch code of conduct
A government tax incentive programme
questionBank.exp: AML is the set of laws, regulations, and procedures designed to prevent criminals from disguising dirty money — a countermeasure framework, not a product, incentive, or voluntary code.

questionBank.q: Under the Vienna Convention, converting property known to derive from drug trafficking specifically to hide its origin falls under which limb of the UN's definition?
opts: Disguising ownership despite already clearly knowing the source
Conversion or transfer to conceal illicit origin
Mandatory reporting duty for suspicious transactions filed
Lawful transfer of property received by inheritance
questionBank.exp: The first Vienna Convention limb addresses converting or transferring property known to derive from drug trafficking to conceal its illicit origin; the second limb instead covers concealing ownership despite already knowing the source.

questionBank.q: Which activity fits the Vienna Convention's second limb, which applies even when the launderer already knows the property's true source?
opts: Disclosing full ownership history to a regulator
Disguising the true nature or ownership of property
Verifying source-of-funds evidence before accepting new deposits
Filing an accurate and complete annual tax return
questionBank.exp: The second limb covers concealing or disguising the true nature, source, location, disposition, movement, or ownership of property, even where the source is already known — distinct from the first limb's focus on conversion or transfer.

questionBank.q: Which activity constitutes Combating the Financing of Terrorism (CFT)?
opts: Auditing a bank's annual accounts
Deterring funding sources for ideological causes
Negotiating and renegotiating corporate loan interest rates
Segmenting customers by preferred channel
questionBank.exp: CFT is investigating, analyzing, deterring, and preventing sources of funding intended to achieve political, religious, or ideological goals — a distinct discipline from routine banking functions.

questionBank.q: According to the training material, terror organizations typically obtain funding from which source?
opts: Direct salaries paid by foreign agencies
Sympathizers among people and organizations
Compulsory levies collected by tax authorities
Insurance payouts following a declared war
questionBank.exp: Referenced Canadian Police Research found terror organizations usually benefit from financing by people and organizations sympathetic to their cause, not from formal state or institutional payments.

questionBank.q: A bank's KYC policy requires establishing a customer's identity, suitability, and risk profile. What concept does this describe?
opts: Anti-Money Laundering legislation
Know Your Customer
FATF's full set of 40 Recommendations
Customer relationship marketing
questionBank.exp: KYC means the bank should know the customer's identity, suitability to be associated with the bank, and the risks around them — distinct from AML law itself or a marketing strategy.

questionBank.q: Understanding a customer's business type, client base, and operating resources — beyond the customer's personal identity — describes which concept?
opts: Anti-Money Laundering procedure
Know Your Customer's Business
Suspicious Transaction Reporting
Combating the Financing of Terrorism
questionBank.exp: KYCB extends KYC to the customer's business itself — its type, clients, and resources — whereas AML, STR, and CFT sit at different stages of the compliance framework.

questionBank.q: Why does a bank invest resources in knowing its customers and their businesses?
opts: To reduce the volume of account paperwork
To avoid legal, licensing, and reputational risk
To increase the volume of cross-sold products
To satisfy customer preferences for faster service
questionBank.exp: The stated rationale is avoiding legal problems for the bank and staff, loss of banking licence, reputational damage, and profitability risk — not operational convenience or sales targets.

questionBank.q: How does 'loss of banking licence' differ from 'legal problems for the bank' as separate listed risks?
opts: Both risks describe the same regulatory outcome
Licence loss is regulatory withdrawal, not liability exposure
Legal problems apply only to individual staff
Licence loss is a category of reputational risk
questionBank.exp: Legal problems concern liability and litigation exposure, while licence loss is a regulator withdrawing the bank's authority to operate — two distinct failure modes tracked separately in the material.

questionBank.q: Which of these appears among the Money Laundering Offences listed in the training material?
opts: Licensed bureau-de-change exchange
Insider trading
Accurate corporate tax filing
Auction purchase of treasury bills
questionBank.exp: Insider trading is explicitly listed as a Money Laundering Offence, alongside illegal arms sales, smuggling, bribery, drug trafficking, embezzlement, tax evasion, and fraud. The other options describe lawful routine activity.

questionBank.q: Which listed Money Laundering Offence involves illegally moving arms, people, or goods across borders?
opts: Concealing taxable income
Smuggling
Misusing non-public market data
Misappropriating entrusted funds
questionBank.exp: Smuggling is listed as illegal cross-border movement of arms, people, or goods — distinct from tax evasion (concealing taxable income), insider trading (misusing market information), or embezzlement (misappropriating entrusted funds).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT listed among the Money Laundering Offences?
opts: Human trafficking operations
Standard mortgage underwriting
Bribery of officials
Financial fraud schemes
questionBank.exp: Human trafficking, bribery, and fraud are all explicitly listed ML offences. Standard mortgage underwriting is a routine, lawful banking function absent from that list.

questionBank.q: A donation from a profit-making organization sympathetic to a terrorist cause is classified under which source category?
opts: Illegal, matching every terrorism-linked funding source
Legal, since the donor's activity is lawful
A formal reporting exemption under CBN rules
A placement-stage transaction needing no scrutiny
questionBank.exp: Donations from non-profit or profit-making organizations sympathetic to terrorists are classified as legal sources — the donor's underlying business is lawful, which is precisely what makes this harder to detect than illegal-source funding.

questionBank.q: Ransom paid to kidnappers who then fund a terrorist organization is classified under which source category?
opts: Legal, treated purely as a private civil matter
Illegal, arising directly from a criminal act
A formal Terrorism Prevention Act exemption
A placement-stage transaction needing no scrutiny
questionBank.exp: Ransom for kidnapping is listed under illegal sources of terrorist financing — proceeds of criminal activity by terrorists or sympathizers — alongside trafficking, imposed levies, and natural-resource exploitation.

questionBank.q: Which pairing correctly matches a funding channel with its source-category classification?
opts: Levy imposed by a terrorist group — legal source
Exploiting oil and gas resources — illegal source
Non-profit donation — illegal source
Profit-organization donation — illegal source
questionBank.exp: Exploiting natural resources such as oil and gas is listed under illegal sources, alongside trafficking and ransom. Donations from non-profit and profit-making organizations are legal-source, and imposed levies are also illegal-source, not legal-source.

questionBank.q: Which group is identified among the 'Big Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism Players'?
opts: Regulated bureau-de-change operators
Public officials
Statutory external auditors
Retail salary-deposit customers
questionBank.exp: Public officials are explicitly listed among the Big Players, alongside drug dealers, mobsters/gang members, politicians, embezzlers, and terrorists — a category defined by illicit-proceeds channels, not routine regulated roles.

questionBank.q: Which 'Big Players' category is distinguished from 'politicians' by holding an administrative rather than elected role?
opts: Mobsters or gang members
Public officials
Drug dealers
Terrorists
questionBank.exp: The material lists 'politicians' and 'public officials' separately — politicians typically hold elected office, public officials hold administrative or civil-service positions — both potential channels for illicit funds.

questionBank.q: A wealthy new client routes funds through shell purchases with no clear economic purpose and has a prior embezzlement conviction. Which Big Player category fits best?
opts: Terrorists
Embezzlers
Mobsters or gang members
Public officials
questionBank.exp: Embezzlers are a listed Big Player category — individuals who misappropriate entrusted funds and then need to disguise the proceeds, matching this client's profile more closely than the other categories.

questionBank.q: Boko Haram's operations in Nigeria are cited in the material as an example of which concept?
opts: Regional regulatory cooperation
Terrorism
A used-car laundering case
A legally exempt donation
questionBank.exp: Boko Haram's operations, alongside the September 11 attacks and ISIS activity, are cited purely as an example of terrorism — the real-world activity CFT measures target — not as a regulatory or case-study example.

questionBank.q: A memo conflates 'money laundering' with 'anti-money laundering.' What is the accurate distinction?
opts: The two terms are used interchangeably in practice
Laundering is the crime; AML is the countermeasure
Laundering is defined as covering only terrorism financing
AML rules are defined to apply only to offshore accounts
questionBank.exp: Money laundering is the offence of disguising illegal proceeds; anti-money laundering is the framework of laws and procedures built to stop it. Scoping either term to a single crime type or account category misstates the definitions.

questionBank.q: A trainee argues CFT and AML are the same discipline. What actually distinguishes CFT from AML?
opts: CFT applies only to domestic transfers
CFT targets ideological funding specifically
CFT is voluntary; AML is legally binding
The two terms are fully interchangeable
questionBank.exp: CFT specifically targets funding sources for politically, religiously, or ideologically motivated activity, while AML addresses disguising crime proceeds more broadly — a narrower purpose-driven focus versus a broader proceeds-of-crime focus.

questionBank.q: Which pair of listed ML offences involves deceiving a market or tax authority rather than physically trafficking goods or people?
opts: Smuggling and human trafficking
Insider trading and tax evasion
Illegal arms sales and drug trafficking
Prostitution and kidnapping
questionBank.exp: Insider trading (misusing non-public market information) and tax evasion (concealing taxable income) both involve deceiving an institution or authority, unlike the trafficking- and smuggling-type offences in the other options.

questionBank.q: Why is a sympathetic non-profit's donation harder to detect as terrorist financing than drug-trafficking proceeds are?
opts: Non-profit donations carry blanket exemption
The underlying activity is itself lawful
Non-profits are never high-risk customers
Drug proceeds are always self-reported
questionBank.exp: Because the donor organization's core activity is lawful, the funds don't display the overt red flags — unclear sourcing, cash-intensive patterns — typical of drug-trafficking proceeds, making legal-source terrorist financing inherently harder to distinguish from ordinary giving.

questionBank.q: A client transfers known drug-trafficking proceeds into a new company name specifically to hide their origin. Which Vienna Convention limb does this illustrate?
opts: Concealing ownership despite already knowing the source
Conversion or transfer to conceal origin
FATF's customer due-diligence recommendation framework
The CBN's three-tiered KYC approach
questionBank.exp: This describes converting/transferring property known to derive from drug trafficking specifically to conceal its illicit origin — the first Vienna Convention limb — rather than a later, separate act of ownership concealment or an unrelated KYC/FATF framework.

questionBank.q: A bank is deciding whether a routine, documented salary deposit needs the same scrutiny as an unexplained large cash lodgment. What should guide that decision?
opts: Applying identical scrutiny to all transactions
Calibrating scrutiny to actual risk exposure
Applying scrutiny only above N50,000
Basing scrutiny solely on customer tenure
questionBank.exp: The rationale for knowing customers and their businesses is managing legal, licensing, reputational, and profitability risk — meaning scrutiny should track the risk a transaction actually poses, not apply uniformly or turn on an unrelated factor like tenure.

questionBank.q: Why does the material list 'public officials' and 'politicians' as separate Big Player categories rather than merging them?
opts: Both categories carry identical risk
They mark distinct channels into illicit finance
Public officials can never be PEPs
The distinction only matters for tax rules
questionBank.exp: Keeping the categories separate preserves a useful distinction between two different institutional channels — elected office versus administrative/civil-service office — that matters for tracing which channel a red flag or PEP designation is coming through.

questionBank.q: A trainee claims insider trading and drug trafficking must involve the same underlying misconduct since both appear on the ML offences list. Is this reasoning sound?
opts: Yes, the list only covers physical goods
No, the list groups by shared consequence
Yes, both share one regulatory body
No, insider trading is not on the list
questionBank.exp: The Money Laundering Offences list groups activities united by producing illegal proceeds that need disguising, not by a shared method. Insider trading (market abuse) and drug trafficking (narcotics crime) are different offences that both generate proceeds requiring laundering.

questionBank.q: A customer receives funds from a foreign non-profit with unclear beneficiaries, and separately from a known kidnapping ransom. How should these be classified under the legal/illegal source framework?
opts: Both treated as illegal-source funding
Donation legal-source; ransom illegal-source
Donation illegal; ransom treated as legal
Neither counts without a border crossing
questionBank.exp: A lawfully constituted donor organization's donation can fall under legal sources even if its use is troubling, whereas ransom for kidnapping is explicitly listed as an illegal source because it arises directly from a criminal act.

questionBank.q: Why does the material treat KYC as foundational to both AML and CFT rather than as a separate discipline?
opts: KYC is unrelated to AML and CFT work
KYC enables recognizing AML/CFT red flags
KYC only matters after an STR is filed
AML and CFT need no customer identification
questionBank.exp: KYC is foundational because establishing true identity and understanding a customer's business is the precondition for recognizing the red flags, high-risk profiles, and suspicious patterns that AML and CFT frameworks exist to catch — not a downstream or unrelated function.

questionBank.q: A criminal group kidnaps a wealthy businessman for ransom and later needs to disguise the ransom proceeds. Which category does the original offence belong to?
opts: A criminal activity that usually leads to money laundering
A routine collections dispute
A civil breach of contract
A regulatory licensing infraction
questionBank.exp: Kidnapping is explicitly listed among the criminal activities that usually lead to money laundering, since proceeds from an illegal act must be disguised to avoid arrest and litigation.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed among the criminal activities that usually lead to Money Laundering?
opts: Counterfeiting
Routine loan repayment
Standard payroll processing
Regulatory stress testing
questionBank.exp: Counterfeiting is explicitly listed among the criminal activities that usually lead to money laundering, alongside kidnapping, extortion, drug trafficking, and forgery. The other options describe routine, lawful bank operations.

questionBank.q: Which pair of criminal activities both involve producing or altering documents or currency dishonestly?
opts: Counterfeiting and forgery
Kidnapping and extortion
Gambling and cheating
Robbery and smuggling
questionBank.exp: Counterfeiting (producing fake currency or goods) and forgery (falsifying documents) both involve dishonest production or alteration, distinguishing them from the coercion-based, chance-based, or theft-based offences in the other pairings.

questionBank.q: At which stage of money laundering is illegal money broken into small units and introduced into the financial system?
opts: Integration
Placement
Layering
Regulatory Reporting
questionBank.exp: Placement is the first stage, where illegal money is broken into small units and introduced into the financial system — distinct from Layering (moving funds through complex transactions) and Integration (funds re-entering the legitimate economy).

questionBank.q: Which stage of money laundering involves converting money into smaller investments and buying goods to obscure its trail?
opts: Placement
Layering
Integration
Fraud Detection
questionBank.exp: Layering is the stage where money is converted into smaller investments and goods are bought, separating the funds from their criminal source through complex transactions — distinct from Placement (initial entry) and Integration (final re-entry).

questionBank.q: At which stage of money laundering do funds re-enter the legitimate economy, for example through real estate purchases?
opts: Placement
Integration
Layering
Credit Screening
questionBank.exp: Integration is the final stage, where funds re-enter the legitimate economy — for example through real estate — after having been placed and layered. Placement and Layering are the earlier stages, and screening is not a named ML stage.

questionBank.q: A launderer makes several smaller cash deposits across multiple bank branches to avoid drawing attention. Which stage of money laundering does this transaction sample represent?
opts: Integration
Placement
Layering
Account Consolidation
questionBank.exp: Smaller cash deposits in banks are listed as a Placement-stage transaction sample — the initial entry of illegal money into the financial system in reduced units to avoid detection.

questionBank.q: A launderer issues several complex bank transfers between shell entities before the funds settle anywhere permanent. Which stage does this represent?
opts: Placement
Layering
Integration
Cash Withdrawal
questionBank.exp: Issuing several complex bank transfers is listed as a Layering-stage transaction sample — designed to separate the funds from their criminal origin through complexity, distinct from the initial Placement or final Integration stage.

questionBank.q: A launderer uses fully layered funds to purchase valuable real estate and finance a legitimate business project. Which stage does this represent?
opts: Placement
Integration
Layering
Credit Screening
questionBank.exp: Purchasing valuable assets, properties, and financing business projects are listed as Integration-stage transaction samples — the final stage where laundered funds re-enter the legitimate economy.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a Placement-stage transaction sample?
opts: Buying and reselling shares
Smuggling money over borders
Purchasing valuable artworks
Debt repayment through credit cards
questionBank.exp: Smuggling money over borders is listed as a Placement-stage sample, alongside smaller cash deposits and lodging bank drafts. Buying/reselling shares and debt repayment are Layering-stage samples, and purchasing artworks is an Integration-stage sample.

questionBank.q: Which category of institution is listed among the 'Non-Bank Institutions' popularly used for money laundering?
opts: Deposit money banks
Money transfer companies
Correspondent banks
Private banking divisions
questionBank.exp: Money transfer companies are listed under Non-Bank Institutions, alongside exchange companies, insurance companies, stockbrokers, and securities traders. Deposit money banks, correspondent banks, and private banking are listed under Banks and Investment Institutions instead.

questionBank.q: Which category of institution is listed among the 'Non-Financial Institutions' popularly used for money laundering?
opts: Discount house products
Real estate firms
Securities traders
Insurance companies
questionBank.exp: Real estate firms are listed under Non-Financial Institutions, alongside casinos, precious-stone traders, car dealers, law/audit firms, and the forex black market. The other options are listed under Non-Bank Institutions instead.

questionBank.q: According to the material, roughly how much money is laundered globally each year?
opts: Between $10 million and $50 million dollars
Between $800 billion and $2 trillion
Between $1 million and $5 million
Between $100 billion and $150 billion
questionBank.exp: The material states that between $800 billion and $2 trillion is laundered in the world annually, with the US making up at least $300 billion of that figure.

questionBank.q: According to the material, the United States accounts for approximately how much of the global annual money laundering figure?
opts: At least $50 billion
At least $300 billion
At least $900 billion
At least $1.5 trillion overall
questionBank.exp: The material states the US makes up at least $300 billion of the $800 billion to $2 trillion laundered globally each year.

questionBank.q: Which economic indicator is listed as something affected countries cannot control due to the scale of global money laundering?
opts: Literacy rates
Inflation rates
Population growth rates
Rainfall patterns
questionBank.exp: The material lists inflation rates, FX rates, and interest rates as indicators that affected countries cannot control due to the scale of the global money laundering problem — not demographic or environmental indicators.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a characteristic of a country that is fertile ground for money laundering?
opts: Strong judicial enforcement capacity
Low risk of detection
Transparent beneficial-ownership registries
High levels of financial-sector supervision
questionBank.exp: Low risk of detection is explicitly listed as a characteristic of fertile countries for money laundering, alongside available financial infrastructure, an unstable economic environment, absence of law, and possible government involvement — the opposite of strong enforcement, transparency, or supervision.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed among the characteristics of countries fertile for money laundering?
opts: A well-funded, fully independent national judiciary system notably
Absence of law and easy tax evasion
Mandatory and comprehensive beneficial-ownership disclosure requirements
Robust and extensive cross-border regulatory information sharing
questionBank.exp: Absence of law and easy tax evasion is explicitly listed as a characteristic of fertile countries for money laundering — the other options describe the kind of institutional strength that would make a country less fertile for laundering, not more.

questionBank.q: Which category is listed among the profiles of High-Risk Customers for money laundering purposes?
opts: Public companies listed on the stock exchange
Private money remitters
Government ministries
Financial institutions themselves
questionBank.exp: Private money remitters are listed among High-Risk Customers, alongside money changers, real estate dealers, casinos, and non-profit organizations/charities. The other options are listed elsewhere as Low-Risk customer categories.

questionBank.q: Which channel is listed among the profiles of High-Risk Channels for money laundering purposes?
opts: In-branch teller cash withdrawal
Correspondent banking
Standing order payments
Cheque clearing through a clearing house
questionBank.exp: Correspondent banking is listed among High-Risk Channels, alongside wire/funds transfers, private banking, and electronic banking services. The other options describe standard, lower-risk retail banking mechanisms.

questionBank.q: Which category is listed among the profiles of High-Risk Countries for money laundering purposes?
opts: Countries with strong anti-corruption enforcement
Drug producing countries
Countries with mandatory ownership registries
Countries with high financial transparency scores
questionBank.exp: Drug producing countries are explicitly listed among High-Risk Countries, alongside countries with high corruption levels and those linked to terrorist financing — the opposite of the enforcement and transparency characteristics in the other options.

questionBank.q: Which statutory basis is cited for the rationale that all financial institutions render services that may be exploited for money laundering?
opts: Section 14 of the Terrorism Prevention Act
Section 25 of the ML Act 2011
Section 17 of the Terrorism Prevention Act
The CBN Tiered KYC Circular
questionBank.exp: The rationale cites Section 25 of the ML Act 2011 as defining the financial services that financial institutions render — the basis for regulatory focus on banks and financial institutions, distinct from the Terrorism Prevention Act sections or the KYC circular.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a rationale for regulatory focus specifically on banks and financial institutions?
opts: Banks employ the highest number of staff nationally
All financial transactions pass through financial institutions
Banks generate the largest tax revenue for government
Banks have the lowest customer complaint rates
questionBank.exp: The material lists 'all financial transactions pass through financial institutions' as a rationale for regulatory focus, alongside financial institutions being the hub of the economy and having exploitable products/services — not staffing levels, tax contribution, or complaint statistics.

questionBank.q: Which impact of money laundering on society is explicitly listed in the material?
opts: Reduced government borrowing costs
Increased country's risk rating
Improved investor confidence
Strengthened judicial independence
questionBank.exp: Increased country's risk rating is explicitly listed as a societal impact of ML/FT, alongside corrupting the value system, financing terrorism, reputational damage, and moral decadence — not the positive outcomes in the other options.

questionBank.q: Which impact of money laundering on Economic Development is explicitly listed in the material?
opts: Increased foreign direct investment
Capital flight and tax evasion
Stronger currency stability
Lower government debt servicing costs
questionBank.exp: Capital flight and tax evasion are explicitly listed as an economic development impact of ML, alongside economic disruption, risks to privatization, stifled competition, and distorted macroeconomic indices — not the positive economic outcomes in the other options.

questionBank.q: Which impact of money laundering on Financial Institutions is explicitly listed in the material?
opts: Improved overall market integrity
Legal risks for banks
Higher customer retention rates
Lower ongoing annual compliance costs
questionBank.exp: Legal risks for banks are explicitly listed as a financial-institution impact of ML, alongside loss of market integrity, negative ethical impacts, and banks' complicity with criminals — not the positive outcomes in the other options.

questionBank.q: Which of the following historical fine examples is cited in the material as one of the highest imposed on a financial institution for money laundering?
opts: A $500,000 fine on a regional credit union
A $31.3 billion fine on J.P. Morgan Chase
A $10,000 fine on a licensed bureau de change
A $2,000 fine on an individual customer
questionBank.exp: The material cites J.P. Morgan Chase's $31.3 billion fine as the largest among the listed high-profile money laundering fines, alongside HSBC ($3.5 billion), BNP Paribas ($2.99 billion), Goldman Sachs ($2.2 billion), RBS ($1.5 billion), and Standard Chartered ($1 billion).

questionBank.q: According to the African financial institution fines table, which institution was penalized for non-compliance with the Financial Intelligence Act (FICA)?
opts: Nedbank Ltd.
Capitec Bank
Standard Bank
Guaranty Trust Bank (UK)
questionBank.exp: Capitec Bank's approximately $3.1 million penalty in 2024 is listed as arising from non-compliance with South Africa's Financial Intelligence Act (FICA), distinct from Nedbank's cash transaction reporting failure and the other listed institutions' compliance failures.

questionBank.q: According to the African fines table, which institution's penalty resulted from a repeat offence in AML weakness and controls?
opts: Standard Chartered located in Mauritius
Guaranty Trust Bank (UK)
Standard Bank of Africa
Nedbank Limited entity
questionBank.exp: Guaranty Trust Bank (UK)'s 2023 penalty is listed as arising from a repeat offence in AML weakness and controls under the UK's FCA, distinct from the failures listed for the other institutions in the table.

questionBank.q: A regulator reviewing the African fines table notices Standard Chartered (Mauritius) was penalized for a specific compliance gap. Which gap was it?
opts: Failure to report suspicious transactions on time
Failure to identify beneficial owners
Non-compliance with cash transaction reporting
Failure to file annual audited accounts
questionBank.exp: Standard Chartered (Mauritius)'s 2021 penalty is listed as arising from failure to identify beneficial owners under the Bank of Mauritius, distinct from Standard Bank's late suspicious-transaction reporting and Nedbank's cash-transaction reporting failure.

questionBank.q: A compliance trainer wants to illustrate why regulators target banks specifically rather than every business in the economy. Which listed rationale best supports that focus?
opts: Banks are the only businesses in any economy that employ dedicated compliance officers
Financial institutions are the hub of the economy through which all financial transactions pass
Banks are the only entities ever subject to government regulation of any kind
Banks generate the highest customer satisfaction scores of any sector nationally
questionBank.exp: The material's rationale is that financial institutions are the hub of the economy and all financial transactions pass through them — a structural reason for regulatory focus, not one based on staffing, exclusivity of regulation, or satisfaction metrics.

questionBank.q: A launderer smuggles cash across a border, later buys and resells shares through several jurisdictions, and finally purchases equity in a legitimate company. Which sequence of stages does this describe?
opts: Integration, then Layering, then Placement
Placement, then Layering, then Integration
Layering, then Placement, then final Integration
Placement, then Integration, then Layering
questionBank.exp: Smuggling cash across a border is a Placement sample, buying/reselling shares across jurisdictions is a Layering sample, and purchasing equity is an Integration sample — matching the correct order Placement, Layering, Integration.

questionBank.q: A bank's compliance officer must decide whether a real estate firm client should be treated as a High-Risk Customer under the material's classification. What should determine that decision?
opts: Whether the client has been a customer for over five years
Whether real estate firms appear on the High-Risk Customer profile
Whether the client's office is located in the bank's home city
Whether the client uses online banking exclusively
questionBank.exp: Real estate dealers are explicitly listed among High-Risk Customers, so classification should follow that listed profile rather than unrelated factors like tenure, location, or channel preference.

questionBank.q: Why does the material link an 'unstable economic environment' to a country being fertile ground for money laundering, rather than treating it as an unrelated economic condition?
opts: Unstable economies always develop stronger anti-corruption enforcement
Instability makes illicit flows harder to distinguish from ordinary volatility
Unstable economies are automatically and permanently exempt from FATF monitoring
Instability guarantees lower detection risk across every transaction type
questionBank.exp: An unstable economic environment is listed as a fertility characteristic because volatile legitimate economic activity makes it harder for regulators or banks to distinguish illicit flows from ordinary economic noise — not because of automatic exemptions or enforcement effects.

questionBank.q: A junior analyst assumes the $800 billion–$2 trillion global laundering estimate represents money that can still be used for national budgets. Is this assumption correct?
opts: Yes, laundered funds eventually enter national treasury accounts formally
No, laundered funds happen outside the economic range and cannot fund national budgets
Yes, but only in countries with unusually strong financial sector infrastructure
No, because the estimate only covers terrorism financing figures and nothing else
questionBank.exp: The material notes that this scale of money laundering happens outside the normal economic range and cannot be used for national budgets — the funds remain hidden from legitimate fiscal use rather than eventually entering national treasuries.

questionBank.q: A bank argues that because its correspondent banking relationships are with reputable foreign banks, the channel itself carries no elevated risk. Does the material's classification support this argument?
opts: Yes, correspondent banking is listed as a Low-Risk channel category
No, correspondent banking is listed High-Risk regardless of counterparty reputation
Yes, but only for relationships confined within the exact same country
No, but only due to currency conversion costs involved here
questionBank.exp: Correspondent banking is explicitly listed as a High-Risk channel in the material's classification — the channel's structural characteristics (limited visibility into underlying customers) create elevated risk independent of how reputable a given counterparty bank is.

questionBank.q: Comparing the JP Morgan Chase and Standard Chartered fine amounts listed in the material, what can be concluded about the scale of penalties across major institutions for money laundering violations?
opts: Penalties are always strictly proportional to the institution's total global headcount
Penalty amounts vary substantially, from around $1 billion to over $31 billion
All listed institutions received exactly identical penalty amounts every single time without exception
Penalties listed apply only to institutions headquartered in America itself
questionBank.exp: The material's list of fines ranges from Standard Chartered's $1 billion to JP Morgan Chase's $31.3 billion, showing substantial variation in penalty scale across institutions rather than uniform, headcount-proportional, or US-only penalties.

questionBank.q: A compliance officer notices that both the global fines table and the African fines table include entries for 'Standard Chartered.' What does comparing these two entries illustrate?
opts: Standard Chartered has never faced any AML penalty outside Africa
Standard Chartered has faced AML-related penalties in more than one jurisdiction
The two entries actually refer to two unrelated, entirely differently named institutions
African penalties are always larger than global penalty examples
questionBank.exp: Standard Chartered appears in both the global fines list ($1 billion) and the African fines list (Mauritius, $120k) in the material, illustrating that the same institution can face AML-related penalties across multiple jurisdictions and regulators.

questionBank.q: A regulator is deciding how much weight to give 'absence of law' versus 'government involvement' when assessing whether a country is fertile ground for money laundering. What does the material suggest about these two factors?
opts: Only one of the two factors can apply to a country at any given time
Both factors are listed independently and can compound each other's effect
Government involvement cancels out the effect of absence of law
Neither factor is relevant unless drug production is also present
questionBank.exp: The material lists absence of law/easy tax evasion and possible government involvement as separate, independent characteristics of fertile countries — both can be present simultaneously and compound rather than cancel or require each other.

questionBank.q: A bank must classify a customer who is both a private banking client and a non-resident. Applying the material's high-risk customer classification, what is the correct approach?
opts: Treat the customer as low risk, since private banking implies strong prior vetting occurred
Treat as high risk, since both private banking and non-resident status are separately listed high-risk factors
Treat as medium risk, since the two factors offset one another entirely
Disregard both factors unless the customer later requests a loan facility
